tool.name: Parse table row into workflow parameters
tool.description: Turn the leading columns of a single table row into typed workflow parameters.

param.label: Input table
param.help: Table with a header row. Exactly one row of this table is parsed into workflow parameters.

param.label: Column delimiter
param.help: Delimiter used by the input table.

param.label: Data row
param.help: Which data row of the table to parse. 1 is the first row below the header. Combine with a rules-based dataset collection to drive a workflow over many rows.

param.name: column_type
param.label: Type
param.help: Type of the generated workflow parameter. This entry describes the column of the table at its position here, so configure the entries in the order the columns appear in the file. Booleans accept true/false, yes/no and 1/0 in any case.

tool.help:
.. class:: infomark
**What it does**
This tool reads **one row** of a CSV or tabular file and turns its columns into **typed workflow parameters** (float, integer, text or boolean). Each output appears in the workflow editor as a connection point that can be attached to the input of a downstream tool, which makes the tool useful for parameter sweeps: keep one row per parameter set in a table and feed the workflow with it.
This is the generic counterpart of ``recetox-aplcms - parse parameters``, which hard-codes the recetox-aplcms column names and types.
Usage .....
**Input**
- **Input table**: a CSV or tabular file with a header row. - **Column delimiter** and **Data row**: how the table is read. Data row 1 is the row directly below the header. - **Column**: one entry per value to extract, given as its type. Configure the entries in the order the columns appear in the file.
**Output**
One parameter per configured column, validated against the selected type. The tool fails with a message naming the offending column instead of coercing it. Booleans accept ``true``/``false``, ``yes``/``no`` and ``1``/``0`` in any case.
Columns are matched **by position**, not by name: the first entry you configure describes the first column of the table, the second entry the second column, and so on. Configure fewer entries than the table has columns and the trailing columns are ignored, which is how you use only part of a parameter table.
.. class:: warningmark
Because matching is positional, the order of your configured entries has to match the column order of the table. A mismatch surfaces as a parse error naming the column, since the header is still read and reported.
The **Data row** parameter pairs well with rules-based dataset collections: build one dataset per parameter set, or point the tool at successive rows of a single table, and let the collection drive the workflow.
Limitation - fixed number of slots ..................................
Galaxy requires a tool to declare its outputs statically, so the number of outputs cannot grow and shrink freely with the number of configured columns. This tool works around that by declaring a pool of **@MAX_SLOTS@ slots** and hiding the unused ones with output filters, which has three visible consequences:
- At most @MAX_SLOTS@ columns can be parsed per invocation; configuring more is an error. - The connection points shown in the workflow editor follow the configured columns, so adding or removing a column can change which downstream inputs are available. - Slots are positional, so output names are generic (``float_0``, ``boolean_3``, ...) and carry the slot index rather than a column name.
